extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for making, documenting, and rebutting obviousness determinations under 35 U.S.C. 103, including the Graham factual inquiries, search scope, rationales supporting obviousness, applicant reply procedures, and consideration of rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiry — scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the scope and content of the prior art by obtaining a thorough understanding of the invention disclosed and claimed (reading the specification and claims) and giving the claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once claim scope is determined, decide what to search for and where to search. The search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed. Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching/suggestion to combine, a preferred search will look for such references if they exist. See MPEP §§ 904, 904.02, 904.03 and § 2111 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiry — differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claims per MPEP § 2111 and consider the totality of the claimed invention and reference teachings (see MPEP § 2141.02). All claim limitations must be considered in comparing to the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiry — level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; a finding on skill may be explicit or implicit in view of the prior art applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors that may be considered include: (1) type of problems encountered in the art; (2) prior art solutions to those problems; (3) rapidity with which innovations are made; (4) sophistication of the technology; and (5) educational level of active workers in the field (In re GPAC). In a given case not every factor will be present and one or more may predominate. Examiners may rely on their own technical expertise; examiners and Board judges are 'persons of scientific competence' and are assumed familiar with the level of skill in their fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective evidence) in obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence relevant to obviousness (secondary considerations) must be evaluated, e.g., commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be included in the specification as filed or presented timely during prosecution. The weight to be given is case-by-case; mere presentation of evidence is not dispositive. Examiners must consider rebuttal evidence when reevaluating an obviousness determination (see MPEP § 2145).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel as factfinders — requirement to articulate findings and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must make and record factual findings concerning the state of the art and the teachings of the references applied; once findings are articulated, provide an explanation to support an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 132 requires that the applicant be notified of the reasons for rejection. Rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning (citing In re Kahn and KSR). Findings may include how a person of ordinary skill would have understood the references.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for in obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred searches will also look for references that provide a teaching, suggestion, or motivation to combine if they exist. See MPEP § 904.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search / analogous art
rubrics_metrics.description: For 35 U.S.C. 103, prior art can be in the field of the applicant's endeavor or be reasonably pertinent to the particular problem with which the applicant was concerned (analogous art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art from other fields or that solves a different problem may be considered if design incentives, market forces, or predictable variations would have prompted a person of ordinary skill to apply it (citing KSR). See MPEP § 2141.01(a) and §§ 901–901.06(d), 2121–2129 for what constitutes prior art and analogous art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Phillips v. AWH Corp. and MPEP § 2111. Determination of claim scope precedes searching and comparison to prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: TSM is a valid rationale to support an obviousness rejection when the prior art provides a teaching, suggestion or motivation to combine, though it should not be applied rigidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR recognized that TSM 'captured a helpful insight' and is not inconsistent with Graham analysis. Examiners may rely on TSM when appropriate but may also use other rationales. See MPEP § 2143 and cited case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Combining prior art elements to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be obvious where prior art elements are combined according to known methods to yield predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an exemplified rationale consistent with KSR. The examiner must articulate why the combination would have been predictable and supported by the record. See MPEP § 2143 and § 2144 discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Simple substitution of one known element for another
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported by the simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record should explain why the substitution would have been obvious and predictable to one of ordinary skill (examples and discussion in MPEP §§ 2143–2144).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Use of known technique to improve similar devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a known technique to improve similar devices (methods or products) in the same way can support an obviousness rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person of ordinary skill would recognize that a technique used to improve one device would improve similar devices, using that technique is obvious unless its application is beyond ordinary skill. Articulate why the technique would be applied and its predictable effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method or product) that is ready for improvement to yield predictable results supports obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the device was 'ready for improvement' and that the application of the technique would predictably produce the claimed result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: 'Obvious to try' with finite predictable solutions and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' may support obviousness when choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale requires that solutions be identifiable and predictable; mere experimentation among many unpredictable possibilities does not support obviousness. See MPEP § 2143.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in another field
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations for use in the same or a different field if those variations would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incentives and market forces can motivate cross-field application of known work; examiner should explain why the variation would be predictable. See KSR discussion and MPEP § 2143.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported when there is some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures classical TSM-type reasoning; the examiner should articulate the relevant teaching/suggestion/motivation and explain the path from prior art to claimed invention. See MPEP § 2143.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common sense in obviousness reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense may be invoked to supply a reason to modify or combine prior art, but it must be supported by evidence and reasoned explanation; it is especially scrutinized when the missing limitation goes to the heart of an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR permits common-sense reasoning but requires reasoned explanation and, in some circumstances, supporting evidence (see Arendi v. Apple and Perfect Web cases). Examiners must avoid conclusory generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must explain why differences between prior art and claims would have been obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art references need not teach every claim limitation, but the examiner must explain why the differences would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness (Dann v. Johnston). The gap between prior art and claim cannot be so great as to render the claim nonobvious; provide articulated reasoning supporting the bridge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant reply / traverse requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must distinctly and specifically point out alleged errors in the Office action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection per 37 CFR 1.111(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective traverse to factual findings must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred; mere assertions that the examiner failed to establish a prima facie case or unsupported claims that reliance on common knowledge lacks documentary evidence are not substantively adequate. If applicant does not properly traverse, the examiner may repeat the rejection and make the next action final (see MPEP § 706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence when reevaluating an obviousness determination, including secondary considerations and evidence of unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After rebuttal evidence is presented, examiners should reconsider the initial determination in view of the entire record and review all rejections and proposed rejections for continued viability. Examples of rebuttal: showing combination was not possible by known methods due to technological difficulties; elements in combination do not merely perform the same functions; claimed combination yielded unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners may rely on their technical expertise and inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners and administrative patent judges are persons of scientific competence and may rely on their technical knowledge to describe what a person of ordinary skill would have known or could have done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings as to the level of ordinary skill and understanding of prior art may be informed by examiners' experience and work in the field (citing In re Berg, PowerOasis, Am. Hoist & Derrick). Nevertheless, factual findings should be articulated in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus of obviousness analysis — what a person of ordinary skill would have known and expected
rubrics_metrics.description: The focus should be on what a person of ordinary skill in the pertinent art would have known at the time and what such a person would have reasonably expected to be able to do in view of that knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies regardless of whether the source was documentary prior art, general knowledge in the art, or common sense. The analysis must tie the facts to the legal conclusion under Graham and KSR.
